chapter: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
title: Radio exposure and the Tico label
summary: Salazar says DJs played only Tico records; Machito says rivals had better publicity men and compares it to sitting on the bench.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Now how come? If they couldn't afford you in 1952, how were they able to afford you in 1954? And then you got ahh -- George Goldner gave you a concert "Machito U.S.A.", with Joe Loco which you went across the country. Was it because you wouldn't sign for Tico that you couldn't get into the Palladium?
How come your records weren't being played then until you got on Tico?
Because they had better publicity or better publicity man or whatever you want to call it. You remember Pancho Raymond?
.... the only records he played were by the people that would go to the Tico Tico dances at the Manhattan Center ....
... that he and Gabriel Diaz promoted.

Now, Dick 'Ricardo' Sugar became -- had a fifteen-minute show on WHBI in September, 1948. By the end of the year he had a few Tico recordings of Al Castellanos and then in 1949 he got those recordings of Tito Puente, like "Abaniquito" and "Maina Go" and "La Renta" by Tito Rodriguez; and he would only play those on the Tico and I heard they didn't play Machito or no one else, except those Tico recordings and they didn't start playing you steady until you got on the Tico label. Doesn't that tell you anything?

Yeah, but how could you - I mean fight the, the whatever. It's just a matter you have to be in the -- It's like you playing baseball and you sitting on the bench and somebody with less quality he is playing regularly and you're sitting on the bench.
